title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 310: Giants and Dwarfs: Rethinking the Island Rule
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 310 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Giants and Dwarfs: Rethinking the Island Rule

Paragraph 1. When biologist J. Bristol Foster published a study of island mammals in 1964, he pointed out a fascinating pattern. On isolated ocean islands, small mainland rodents frequently evolved into giants, whereas massive animals like elephants and hippos shrank into dwarfs. Ancient fossils dug up in the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia, and California's Channel Islands revealed pony-sized mammoths and dog-sized rats. For decades, biologists treated 'Foster's Rule' as a neat, universal law of island evolution.

Paragraph 2. In her recent book Islands of Time, researcher Dr. Claire Moreau takes a careful look at Foster's classic theory. Moreau agrees that island isolation has produced amazing evolutionary surprises, yet she argues early scientists tried too quickly to reduce complex nature to a single simple formula. According to Moreau, body size shifts are driven by the balance between freedom from hunters and limited island resources.

Paragraph 3. On large continents, small mammals are constantly hunted by hawks and meat-eating mammals, forcing them to stay small and hide in narrow burrows. Once rodents reach an island free of mammalian predators, they enjoy 'ecological release': freed from hiding underground, larger bodies win the race for food and store energy better. Conversely, giant mainland plant-eaters need huge body mass to defend against wolves and big cats. Because tiny islands cannot support big hunting cats, those giant plant-eaters no longer need massive armour and shrink to survive on scarce island food.

Paragraph 4. However, Moreau's biggest finding challenges the idea that Foster's Rule works everywhere. After studying more than two thousand living and extinct island animal groups using modern genetic data, she proved the rule operates unevenly. While elephants and certain mice fit the rule well, other groups like carnivores and bats show no clear size pattern at all.

Paragraph 5. Furthermore, Moreau discovered that local weather shifts, steep mountain terrain, and the geological age of an island influence animal size far more than simple land area. Her research offers an important lesson: living nature is too diverse and messy to obey neat human rules.

q6.text: How did scientists view Foster's Rule for many decades after 1964?
options: A. As an unproven guess based on fake bones
B. As a general natural law applying to all islands
C. As a rule limited strictly to Mediterranean birds
D. As a temporary effect caused by human farming

steps: Đoạn 1: Từng được coi là quy luật phổ quát (neat, universal law).

q7.text: What mistake did early biologists make according to Dr. Claire Moreau?
options: A. They ignored elephant fossils found in Southeast Asia.
B. They focused solely on ocean fish rather than land mammals.
C. They believed island animals never changed size at all.
D. They turned complex ecological forces into an overly simple formula.

steps: Đoạn 2: Vội vàng thu gọn bản chất sinh thái phức tạp thành một công thức đơn giản.

q8.text: What advantage does larger size give island rodents when predators are absent?
options: A. Better success at winning food and storing energy
B. Greater speed for escaping angry hawks
C. Ability to dig deeper underground tunnels
D. Higher immunity against freezing ocean winds

steps: Đoạn 3: Cơ thể lớn hơn giúp giành thức ăn và tích trữ năng lượng hiệu quả hơn.

q9.text: What did Moreau's study of over 2,000 animal populations prove?
options: A. Human hunting caused every island dwarf to die out.
B. Rodents always shrink when moved to cold islands.
C. Foster's Rule does not operate reliably across all mammal groups.
D. Genetic data cannot explain ancient fossil sizes.

steps: Đoạn 4: Chứng minh quy luật này vận hành không đồng đều (operates unevenly) ở mọi nhóm thú.

q10.text: According to Paragraph 5, which factors affect body size more than island area?
options: A. Ocean wave height and human fishing boats
B. Local weather, rugged terrain, and island age
C. Distance from the nearest desert continent
D. Number of plant-eating reptiles nearby

steps: Đoạn 5: Thời tiết địa phương, địa hình núi dốc và tuổi địa chất của đảo.
